summary: A federal republic in Central Europe, the most populous country and largest economy in the EU; it went through two world wars and East–West division, and was reunified in 1990.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: The non-religious population is concentrated in the former East Germany: from 1949 to 1990 the East German regime promoted atheism, replacing confirmation with the secular “Jugendweihe” (youth dedication), and believers faced pressure in education and employment, so church membership dropped sharply. In the former West Germany, because of postwar secularization, the church tax system (those registered as church members pay a surcharge on income tax) and the church sexual abuse scandals that erupted from 2010, hundreds of thousands of people formally leave the church every year.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: In the 8th century Saint Boniface, the “Apostle of the Germans,” preached in the German lands, and Catholicism became the mainstream faith of the medieval Holy Roman Empire. The Peace of Augsburg in 1555 established the principle “cuius regio, eius religio,” and the southern and western states such as Bavaria and the Rhineland remained Catholic, which is why Catholics are still concentrated in southern and western Germany today. In the 1870s Bismarck launched the “Kulturkampf” to suppress the Catholic Church, which in fact strengthened Catholic political mobilization.

ranking.name: Protestantism (Evangelical Church in Germany)
ranking.description: In 1517 Martin Luther posted his Ninety-five Theses at Wittenberg, setting off the Reformation, and princes in the north and east converted to Lutheranism one after another. In 1817 Prussia merged the Lutheran and Reformed churches into a United Church, and in 1945 the Protestant churches of the states formed the Evangelical Church in Germany (EKD). Because the traditionally Protestant regions lay mostly in the former East Germany, secularization in the communist era caused the Protestant share to fall faster than the Catholic one.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: In 1961 West Germany signed a guest-worker recruitment agreement with Turkey, and large numbers of Turkish workers moved in; after recruitment stopped in 1973 they settled through family reunification, forming Germany’s largest Muslim group. Refugees from the Bosnian war in the 1990s, and about a million asylum seekers from Syria, Afghanistan and Iraq in 2015–2016, increased the Muslim population further, which is distributed mainly in the large cities of the west and the Ruhr region.

ranking.name: Eastern Orthodoxy
ranking.description: Orthodox believers come mainly from immigrants brought in under labor agreements signed in the 1960s with Greece (1960) and Yugoslavia (1968), and later from Romanian and Bulgarian EU migrants and Russian and Ukrainian immigrants, each with its own Greek, Serbian, Romanian and Russian Orthodox churches.

religion.background: The German lands were Christianized in the early Middle Ages through the Frankish kingdom and missionaries; Luther’s Reformation in the 16th century made Germany the birthplace of Protestantism, and after the Thirty Years’ War (1618–1648) a pattern of Protestant north and Catholic south took shape. After unification in the 19th century, conflict and cooperation between church and state coexisted, and the church tax system continues to this day. After World War II East Germany enforced atheism, and after reunification the east became one of the most secular regions in Europe; meanwhile, immigration since the 1960s has brought Islam and Orthodoxy, making Germany’s religious landscape increasingly diverse.

ranking.name: German
ranking.description: German derives from the dialects of the Germanic tribes, and Old High German texts appear from the 8th century. In 1522 Luther translated the New Testament into a German based on Saxon chancery usage, which greatly advanced the unification of the written standard; in the 19th century the Brothers Grimm compiled their great dictionary, and in 1880 Duden published his orthographic dictionary, establishing modern Standard German. Dialects such as Bavarian and Low German are still kept in various regions, but schools and the media use Standard German.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: After the German–Turkish labor recruitment agreement was signed in 1961, Turkish guest workers came to West Germany in large numbers, and after recruitment stopped in 1973 their families moved in and settled; today there are about three million people of Turkish background. Berlin’s Kreuzberg district, Cologne and the Ruhr region have large Turkish-speaking communities, and many second- and third-generation immigrants speak Turkish at home and German outside.

ranking.name: Russian
ranking.description: Russian speakers are mainly “Russian Germans”: in the 18th century Catherine II invited German farmers to settle along the Volga, their descendants were deported in the Soviet era, and around the 1990s more than two million “returned” to Germany as ethnic Germans, many of whom still use Russian as their home language. There are also Soviet Jewish immigrants, and Ukrainian refugees after 2022.

ranking.name: Arabic
ranking.description: The Arabic-speaking community formed in the 1970s and 1980s because of the Lebanese civil war and Palestinian refugees; in the refugee wave of 2015–2016 large numbers of Syrians and Iraqis arrived, quickly making Arabic one of Germany’s main immigrant languages, concentrated in large cities such as Berlin.

ranking.name: Polish
ranking.description: In the late 19th century the coal and steel industries of the Ruhr attracted large numbers of Polish workers, forming the “Ruhr Poles” community. After Poland joined the EU in 2004 and Germany fully opened its labor market in 2011, Polish immigration grew sharply again, and today it is one of the largest immigrant groups in Germany.

language.history: The dialects of the Germanic tribes developed in the Middle Ages into Old High German and Old Low German, and medieval poets wrote in Middle High German. The printing press and Luther’s translated Bible gradually made a written language based on East Central German dialects the common standard across Germany. Nationalism in the 19th century and unification in 1871 further promoted standardization, and dialects retreated to everyday speech. After World War II Germany became a country of immigration, and community languages such as Turkish, Russian, Arabic and Polish appeared in large numbers, while German remains the only nationwide official language.

ranking.name: Bratwurst
ranking.description: A sausage stuffed with ground pork or mixed pork and beef, grilled over charcoal or pan-fried until the skin is browned and fragrant, often served in a small bread roll with mustard.
ranking.history: The “Brät” in the name means finely chopped meat filling, and “Wurst” means sausage. German sausages have a long history: the earliest written record of the Thuringian bratwurst appears in a 1404 document from Arnstadt, while Nuremberg is famed for its finger-sized grilled sausages, which are still protected by designation of origin. The butchers’ guilds of medieval towns set strict recipes, so that more than a thousand regional sausages developed in various places. Today it is an indispensable national snack at football stadiums, Christmas markets and summer barbecues.

ranking.name: Pretzel (Brezel)
ranking.description: Dough is rolled into a long strand and twisted into a crossed knot, dipped in lye solution and sprinkled with coarse salt before baking, giving a dark brown glossy crust and a supple, chewy inside.
ranking.history: The pretzel’s shape is generally thought to originate in medieval monasteries, resembling arms crossed in prayer, and from the 12th century it became the emblem of the bakers’ guilds of southern Germany; to this day many bakeries still hang a pretzel sign at the door. In the past it was often eaten during Lent because the dough contains no egg or butter. Dipping in lye gives the crust its distinctive brown color and flavor, and it is representative of Swabia and Bavaria; at Munich’s Oktoberfest, giant pretzels are indispensable.

ranking.name: Currywurst
ranking.description: A fried or deep-fried pork sausage is cut into pieces and topped with a sauce made of ketchup and curry powder, then sprinkled with another layer of curry powder, and served with fries or bread.
ranking.history: In 1949 Herta Heuwer, a snack-stand owner in Berlin, mixed a sauce from curry powder and ketchup that she had obtained by trade from British troops stationed in Germany and poured it over a sausage, and the currywurst was born; she later even registered a name for the sauce. Postwar Berlin, short of supplies, needed cheap and flavorful food, and the dish quickly became popular among workers and students and spread to the Ruhr industrial region. It symbolizes everyday life in the postwar reconstruction years, and hundreds of millions are sold in Germany every year.

ranking.name: Schweinshaxe (German pork knuckle)
ranking.description: A cured pork hind knuckle is roasted slowly at low temperature for a long time until the skin is crisp and the meat tender, served with potato dumplings and sauerkraut, with beer gravy poured over it.
ranking.history: Schweinshaxe is a traditional Bavarian dish; the pork knuckle is a cheaper cut, and farm families made it delicious through long roasting. It is inseparable from Bavarian beer culture and often appears in beer halls such as Munich’s Hofbräuhaus (founded in 1589) and at Oktoberfest. In northern Germany there is the boiled “Eisbein” version, and the north–south difference reflects the diversity of German regional cuisine.

ranking.name: Black Forest cake (Schwarzwälder Kirschtorte)
ranking.description: Chocolate sponge cake is layered with sour cherries and whipped cream and soaked with Black Forest cherry brandy, decorated on top with chocolate shavings and cherries.
ranking.history: The name comes from the Black Forest region of southwestern Germany, which abounds in cherries and cherry brandy (Kirschwasser); some also believe the design was inspired by the red pom-poms on the traditional hats of local women. The cake is generally believed to have been created by the pastry chef Josef Keller around 1915, began to appear in cookbooks in the 1930s, and after World War II became one of Germany’s most popular cakes, spreading widely around the world. German food guidelines still require that a cake bearing this name must contain cherry brandy.
